title: Ecclesiastes 7:15–29
context: The Preacher reflects on the righteous who perish and the wicked who prosper, warns against excess in either direction, and points to the fear of God. He affirms that no one on earth is without sin, and closes with his search for wisdom, including the difficult sayings about the woman whose heart is snares and ‘one man among a thousand,’ which are reported here as his words and read soberly. He concludes that God made mankind upright, but they have sought many schemes. Both traditions read these lines as shared ground about universal sin, and existing boxes treat their differences.

verses.text: All this I have seen in my days of vanity: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who lives long in his evildoing.
verses.arminianNotes:
In his days of vanity the Preacher has seen a righteous man perish in his righteousness and a wicked man live long in his evil. Life does not always reward virtue.

Arminian readers see honest observation.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse records an exception to the usual pattern of reward, without resolving it.

Reformed readers see the limits of what can be seen under the sun. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the hard reality of apparent injustice.

verses.text: Don’t be overly righteous, neither make yourself overly wise. Why should you destroy yourself?
verses.arminianNotes:
Do not be overly righteous or overly wise; why destroy yourself? The warning is surprising.

Arminian readers often see a caution against self-righteousness or rigid scrupulosity rather than against true goodness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Interpreters differ on what ‘overly righteous’ means; proposals include self-righteous display or a pursuit of righteousness that presumes it can guarantee reward.

Reformed readers see a warning against pride. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Don’t be too wicked, neither be foolish. Why should you die before your time?
verses.arminianNotes:
Do not be too wicked or foolish; why die before your time? The warning balances verse 16.

Arminian readers see that the caution against excess does not license moral carelessness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse does not imply that some wickedness is acceptable; it warns against abandoning restraint.

Reformed readers see sin’s destructive consequences. Both traditions read this as shared ground and read verses 16–17 together, resisting any reading that treats either as permission for wrongdoing.

verses.text: It is good that you should take hold of this. Yes, also don’t withdraw your hand from that; for he who fears God will come out of them all.
verses.arminianNotes:
It is good to grasp this and not let go of that, for whoever fears God will come out of them all. The fear of God guides.

Arminian readers see the fear of God as the way through life’s tensions.
verses.reformedNotes:
The meaning of ‘them all’ is debated, but the fear of God is clearly the answer to the extremes of verses 16–17.

Reformed readers see reverence for God as the root of wisdom. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Wisdom is a strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wisdom strengthens the wise more than ten rulers in a city. Wisdom is a source of strength.

Arminian readers see wisdom as worth seeking, a strength that exceeds what political power alone can give.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image compares wisdom favorably with the combined authority of many rulers.

Reformed readers see wisdom as God’s gift that strengthens his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about wisdom’s value, while the next verse reminds readers that even the wise are not without sin.

verses.text: Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and doesn’t sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin. Universal sinfulness is affirmed.

Arminian readers see sin as universal (compare the boxes at Psalm 51:5 and Romans 5:12).
verses.reformedNotes:
The thought resembles 1 Kings 8:46, and some readers connect it with Paul’s teaching in Romans 3:10–23, discussed at the Romans 3:11 box.

Reformed readers likewise affirm universal sin. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground, and the existing boxes treat their differences.

verses.text: Also don’t take heed to all words that are spoken, lest you hear your servant curse you;
verses.arminianNotes:
Do not take every spoken word to heart, or you may hear your servant curse you. Overhearing invites hurt.

Arminian readers see wisdom in not reacting to every remark, so that a person is not ruled by what others say.
verses.reformedNotes:
The counsel is practical: not every overheard criticism deserves attention.

Reformed readers see humility and grace in bearing others’ words. Both traditions read this as shared ground about patience and restraint, and the next verse grounds it in self-knowledge.

verses.text: for often your own heart knows that you yourself have likewise cursed others.
verses.arminianNotes:
For your own heart knows that you have often cursed others. Self-knowledge humbles.

Arminian readers see honesty about one’s own failings as the ground for bearing with others, a lesson that follows naturally from verse 20.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse applies the universal sinfulness of verse 20 to everyday speech.

Reformed readers see self-examination producing humility and mercy. Both traditions read this as shared ground about recognizing in ourselves the faults we resent in others.

verses.text: All this I have proved in wisdom. I said, “I will be wise;” but it was far from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher has tested all this by wisdom and resolved to be wise, but wisdom was far from him. Wisdom eludes.

Arminian readers see humble honesty about the limits of human understanding, even in one who sought it diligently.
verses.reformedNotes:
The admission that wisdom was ‘far from me’ is striking from one devoted to it.

Reformed readers see the limits of human wisdom pointing to God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about humility in the search for understanding.

verses.text: That which is, is far off and exceedingly deep. Who can find it out?
verses.arminianNotes:
What exists is far off and very deep; who can find it out? Reality exceeds human grasp.

Arminian readers see humility before the depth of God’s world, which invites wonder and trust rather than despair.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse echoes 3:11, where man cannot find out the work God has done.

Reformed readers see God’s ways beyond full human understanding. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the limits of human knowledge before the depth of God’s works.

verses.text: I turned around, and my heart sought to know and to search out, and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know that wickedness is stupidity, and that foolishness is madness.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher turns his heart to know, search, and seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know that wickedness is folly and foolishness madness. The search intensifies.

Arminian readers see diligent moral inquiry.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse introduces the findings of verses 26–29.

Reformed readers see the search exposing the folly of sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of moral inquiry and the conclusion that wickedness is not wise.

verses.text: I find more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and traps, whose hands are chains. Whoever pleases God shall escape from her; but the sinner will be ensnared by her.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Preacher finds more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and whose hands are chains; whoever pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is caught. The warning is severe.

Arminian readers see a warning against entrapment.
verses.reformedNotes:
What the line is doing is debated: proposals include a particular kind of seductive woman, Lady Folly as in Proverbs 9:13, or a figure for sin’s snare. It describes this woman, not all women.

Reformed readers likewise read it soberly. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: “Behold, I have found this,” says the Preacher, “to one another, to find an explanation
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, I have found this,” says the Preacher, adding one thing to another to find an explanation. He reasons step by step.

Arminian readers see careful inquiry, which the Preacher presents as an ongoing and unfinished search.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse frames the findings as the Preacher’s own conclusions, introduced with his name.

Reformed readers see the speaker’s observations recorded honestly. Both traditions read the following lines as his words within the book’s argument, not as a general rule beyond what the text states.

verses.text: which my soul still seeks, but I have not found. I have found one man among a thousand, but I have not found a woman among all those.
verses.arminianNotes:
He is still seeking and has not found; he has found one man among a thousand, but not a woman among all those. The line is puzzling.

Arminian readers do not treat it as a verdict on women.
verses.reformedNotes:
Proposals include rhetorical hyperbole, a reference to the woman of verse 26, or a lament over humanity generally, since verse 29 speaks of mankind. The text does not settle it.

Reformed readers likewise read it soberly. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Behold, I have only found this: that God made mankind upright; but they search for many inventions.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He has found only this: God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes. The fault lies with humanity.

Arminian readers see creation good and sin humanity’s own (compare the boxes at Genesis 8:21 and Romans 5:12).
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse speaks of ‘mankind,’ men and women alike, which may help explain verse 28.

Reformed readers see an upright creation followed by humanity’s fall. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and the existing boxes treat their differences.
